title: War and peace, in context
hookLine: fight those who fight you and don't transgress (2:190), incline to peace (8:61), read with their occasions

lines: A SENTENCE CUT FROM ITS PAGE.
PUT IT BACK ON THE PAGE.
cards: Take any sentence out of a novel and you can make it say almost anything. Take him, says a character, and it sounds like a kidnapping, until you read the page and find it's a chess game.
Scripture can be handled the same way, by anyone, for any purpose. A handful of Qur'an verses about fighting are often clipped and passed around like that. Today, put them back on the page.

teach.b: Start with the setting. For about thirteen years in Mecca, the early Muslims were persecuted and told to be patient; no fighting was permitted.
After the move to Medina, surah twenty-two gives the first permission: to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged.
Then al-Baqarah, verse one hundred ninety, in Pickthall's translation: "Fight in the way of Allah against those who fight against you, but begin not hostilities. Lo! Allah loveth not aggressors."
The next verse, the one most often clipped, says to fight them wherever you meet them. Read on two verses: if they stop, Allah is forgiving, and there's to be no hostility except against wrongdoers.

And al-Anfal, verse sixty-one: "And if they incline to peace, incline thou also to it, and trust in Allah." The hadith add limits too. In al-Bukhari, the Prophet ﷺ forbade the killing of women and children in war.
Muslim scholars built a whole field for this, asbab an-nuzul, the occasions of revelation: what was happening when a verse came down, who it addressed, what came before and after.

They also argued, across centuries, about how these verses fit together and what they mean for later times. The Qur'an doesn't settle every question in one line, and the scholars didn't pretend it did.
A verse has a neighborhood: a situation it came down into, a sentence before it and a sentence after. Reading it alone isn't reading it.

how: Muslim scholars read verses about fighting together with their occasions of revelation (asbab an-nuzul), surrounding verses and hadith, and classical law set limits in war such as the prohibition on harming women and children.

games.q: someone shows you the line fight them wherever you meet them, alone. what do the verses around it add?
o: fight those who fight you, don't aggress, and stop if they stop.
only that it was revealed in Mecca.
games.why: 2:190 limits it to those who fight you and forbids aggression; 2:192–193 say if they stop, hostility ends.

practice: Choose a verse or line you know well, from the Qur'an or from anywhere this year. Ask three questions, slowly: what comes right before it, what comes right after, and when, or to whom, was it first said?
If you don't know, notice that; it isn't a failure, it's the start of reading.
